text: This is what happens inside your body when you get shot.
A handgun bullet travels at around twelve hundred feet per second. Faster than the speed of sound.
When it enters your thigh, it crushes everything in its path, leaving a tunnel of destroyed tissue called the permanent cavity.
It also shoves the muscle outward, creating a temporary cavity that stretches and snaps back in just a few milliseconds.
And no, you won't fly backwards like in the movies. The bullet carries less momentum than a fastball.
Many people don't even feel it at first, because a rush of adrenaline masks the pain.
The real danger is blood loss. If the bullet tears your femoral artery, you could bleed out in just a few minutes.
As your blood volume drops, your heart races, and your brain starts running out of oxygen. This is called hemorrhagic shock.
That's why a tourniquet, tightened a few inches above the wound, can be the difference between life and death.
And surprisingly, doctors often leave the bullet inside you, because removing it could cause even more damage.
